title: California REO Listing Requirements — State-Specific Policy
content:
California REO Clear-To-List Policy — State-Specific Requirements.

Overview: California permits both judicial and non-judicial foreclosure. The majority of residential foreclosures in California are non-judicial, governed by California Civil Code Sections 2924 through 2924k. REO (Real Estate Owned) properties acquired through foreclosure have specific CTL requirements due to California's extensive disclosure mandates and tenant protection laws.

Section 1 — Foreclosure Verification:
Verify the trustee's sale was conducted in compliance with California Civil Code Section 2924. Required steps include: (a) notice of default was recorded with the county recorder, (b) a minimum 90-day reinstatement period elapsed after notice of default, (c) notice of trustee's sale was recorded at least 20 days before sale, posted on the property, and published in a newspaper of general circulation, (d) the sale was conducted as a public auction, and (e) the trustee's deed upon sale has been recorded. For judicial foreclosures, verify the court order and any applicable redemption period (one year for judicial foreclosure under California Code of Civil Procedure Section 729.030).

Section 2 — Tenant Protections:
California provides significant protections for tenants in foreclosed properties. Under California Civil Code Section 2924.8 and the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, bona fide tenants with existing leases are entitled to remain in the property for the duration of their lease or 90 days, whichever is longer. Month-to-month tenants must receive a minimum 90-day notice to vacate. These tenant rights affect the CTL timeline. An occupied REO property with a protected tenant cannot be listed as vacant possession until the notice period expires and the tenant vacates.

Section 3 — Mandatory Hazard Disclosures:
California requires extensive natural hazard disclosures for all real property sales, including REO. Before listing, the following disclosures must be prepared: (a) Natural Hazard Disclosure report identifying whether the property is in a Special Flood Hazard Area, Dam Inundation Zone, Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone, Wildland Area, Earthquake Fault Zone (Alquist-Priolo), or Seismic Hazard Zone, (b) Environmental assessments for properties built before 1978 regarding potential lead-based paint per federal requirements, and (c) any known material facts about the property condition. REO sellers in California cannot claim the as-is exemption for natural hazard disclosures — the NHD report is mandatory regardless of sale type.

Section 4 — SB-1079 Right of First Refusal:
California Senate Bill 1079, codified in California Civil Code Section 2924m, grants eligible tenant occupants, prospective owner-occupants, nonprofit affordable housing organizations, community land trusts, and public entities a right of first refusal on foreclosed residential properties of one to four units. After the trustee's sale, there is a statutory 45-day period during which these eligible bidders may submit offers at or above the last highest bid. The CTL process must account for this waiting period. A property cannot be listed on the open market until the 45-day SB-1079 window has expired without an eligible offer.

Section 5 — Valuation Standards for California:
BPO staleness threshold for California REO properties follows the 90-day baseline. However, AVM variance threshold for California is 10 percent, stricter than the 15 percent baseline. California's real estate markets, particularly in coastal metropolitan areas (Los Angeles, San Francisco Bay Area, San Diego), exhibit higher volatility and price stratification. The tighter AVM threshold ensures valuation accuracy in these dynamic markets. If AVM-to-BPO variance exceeds 10 percent, mandatory valuation review is required.

Section 6 — HOA Super Lien in California:
California Civil Code Section 5680 establishes HOA assessment lien priority. In California, the HOA assessment lien does not have automatic super-priority over a first-lien mortgage (unlike some states such as Nevada). However, HOA liens recorded before the first trust deed may take priority. After acquiring a property through foreclosure, the new owner is responsible for regular assessments going forward. Delinquent pre-foreclosure assessments should be verified. Any HOA transfer fees and document requirements must be compiled before listing.

Section 7 — Los Angeles County Specific:
For properties in Los Angeles County, verify compliance with the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LARSO) for multi-unit properties. Properties subject to rent stabilization have additional tenant relocation requirements and restriction on rent increases. The Los Angeles Housing Department must be contacted for any rent-stabilized units acquired through foreclosure. Additionally, the City of Los Angeles has seismic retrofit requirements for certain soft-story buildings that must be disclosed.

References: California Civil Code Sections 2924-2924k (Non-Judicial Foreclosure), California Civil Code Section 2924m (SB-1079 Right of First Refusal), California Civil Code Section 5680 (HOA Assessment Liens), California Code of Civil Procedure Section 729.030 (Judicial Foreclosure Redemption).
